evidence: Think of it as choosing when the combining work happens. Do it during the nightly load and readers get ready-made rows cheaply, though what they see can only be as new as that load. Do it inside the database on demand and results are always current, at the price of redoing the work per request. Do it in the browser and you pay in extra round trips. Which one is right depends on how stale the consumers can afford to be, so freshness tolerance is the real deciding variable.

curriculum:
### Where the join happens
**Mechanism.** A join can be executed at ETL time, at query time inside the database, or on the client after several fetches. An ETL-time join materialises the combined rows ahead of any read, so the cost is paid once per load instead of once per read, but the result is only as fresh as the last load. The staleness budget the consumers can tolerate therefore decides where the join should live.
**Boundary.** When consumers need read-your-writes freshness, an ETL-time join is the wrong tool.

P1.span: Do it during the nightly load and readers get ready-made rows cheaply, though what they see can only be as new as that load

evidence: The core idea is that a join is a cost you can place at different points in a data flow. Precomputing shifts effort from many reads to one write pass and trades away freshness. Computing on demand keeps things current but repeats effort. Pushing it to the caller distributes the work and adds latency. The design question is therefore how much staleness the readers can tolerate, and the answer selects the placement.

curriculum:
### Where the join happens
**Mechanism.** A join can be executed at ETL time, at query time inside the database, or on the client after several fetches. An ETL-time join materialises the combined rows ahead of any read, so the cost is paid once per load instead of once per read, but the result is only as fresh as the last load. The staleness budget the consumers can tolerate therefore decides where the join should live.
**Boundary.** When consumers need read-your-writes freshness, an ETL-time join is the wrong tool.
